answer: The first century in which Diversity in Pottery Decoration and Diversity in Pottery Form show opposite growth trends is the 18th century BCE, in the window from 1800 BCE to 1700 BCE: Pottery Decoration increases significantly (Z rises from −0.48 at 1800 BCE to 0.97 at 1700 BCE, Δ = +1.45) while Pottery Form simultaneously declines (Z falls from 0.74 to −1.13, Δ = −1.87). This is the only century transition in the whole series (BCE 4300–500) with a simultaneous decoration increase and form decline, hence the first; the change is an order of magnitude larger than the typical century step (median |Δ| ≈ 0.06), so it satisfies any reasonable "significant" threshold (all tested: 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5 and 3×MAD), and the result is identical in both supplied files (capital.csv and the century anchors of time_series_data.csv, which agree at all 37 shared points, 0 mismatches). The state realized at the 1700 BCE anchor then persists: Pottery Form stays flat at −1.13 for the remainder of the series, confirming that the divergence was achieved once and never reversed into the opposite-sign transition.

payload.workflow: Source: capital.csv (ZKeform=Pottery Form, Zkeverz=Pottery Decoration; 39 century anchors BCE 4300→500) as primary table, cross-checked against time_series_data.csv raw values at century anchors (CE=-BCE; 37 shared anchors, 0 mismatches) and *_inter (piecewise-linear, adds nothing at century scale). Growth = absolute first difference of Z between adjacent century anchors, chronologically forward (decreasing BCE). Opposite = dForm<0 AND dDec>0 simultaneously. Significance = |d|>=threshold with sweep {0.1,0.2,0.3,0.5} and 3×MAD. 'First time' = scan from oldest (BCE 4300) to youngest (BCE 500). Result: the only opposite-significant transition is 1800→1700 BCE (dForm=-1.87, dDec=+1.45), robust to all thresholds, confirmed in both files; from 1700 BCE onward Form stays flat (-1.13). Century reported as interval (18th century BCE, 1800–1700 BCE).
